evidence_quote: The average concurrent-flow flame spread rate is 1.8 mm/s. The opposed-flow flame average spread rate 1.3 mm/s.
finding: In the large Saffire-1 fire (40.6-cm-wide fabric, 20 cm/s air flow), the flame spread on average at 1.8 mm/s with the flow (concurrent) and 1.3 mm/s against it (opposed).
conditions: Microgravity, unoccupied ISS resupply vehicle, air flow 20 cm/s

team_interpretation.text: A large fabric fire in a ventilated module keeps spreading steadily; spread with the air flow is faster than against it.

score_reasons.crew_safety: Measured spread of a large cabin-scale fabric fire: the core input for fire-response time planning.
score_reasons.evidence: Measured in orbit; source is conference slides, not the full paper.
score_reasons.moon_mars: Directly relevant to closed habitats and transit vehicles.

evidence_quote: Unlike 1-g, the results revealed that a steady flame could be achieved even for a wide sample burning in concurrent-flow.
finding: A wide fabric sample burning with the air flow in microgravity produced a steady flame, a result the authors contrast with normal gravity.
earth_comparison: The authors state this differs from normal gravity (1-g).

team_interpretation.text: Crews should not expect a cabin fabric fire to die out on its own while ventilation is running.

score_reasons.crew_safety: A steady (not self-limiting) fire means it will not burn out by itself while air flows.
score_reasons.evidence: Conclusion stated by the authors after the in-orbit test.
score_reasons.moon_mars: Applies to any ventilated crew vehicle.

evidence_quote: This behavior of the flame demonstrated the importance of confined spaces for potential spacecraft fires.
finding: Flames in the large Saffire test spread more slowly than in earlier tests in smaller ducts, showing that the size of the confined space matters for spacecraft fires.

team_interpretation.text: Fire models for a new habitat should be checked against large-scale tests, not only small-sample tests.

score_reasons.crew_safety: Means small-duct test data may not predict real cabin fires.
score_reasons.evidence: Qualitative conclusion; comparison data are in other papers.
score_reasons.moon_mars: Habitat volumes differ from test ducts.

evidence_quote: Results were convincing although rather anticlimactic as none of the silicone samples burned.
finding: None of the silicone sheet samples kept burning in microgravity: after the igniter was switched off a tiny flame remained but did not spread and quickly went out.
conditions: Microgravity, moderate forced air flow; igniter turned off after ignition
earth_comparison: Not even the thin sample spread a flame in microgravity, although it was entirely consumed in normal gravity.

team_interpretation.text: Silicone appeared less flammable in these space conditions, but only for the flow speed tested.

score_reasons.crew_safety: Shows a material can be less flammable in space than on Earth.
score_reasons.evidence: Direct in-orbit observation on several samples.

evidence_quote: More work is needed to understand the differences between the normal and micro-g flammability of silicone.
finding: The authors could not explain why silicone burned less in microgravity; possible reasons they give are silica powder covering the fuel and the different (buoyant versus forced) air flow.
open_question: Why is silicone less flammable in microgravity than in normal gravity, and would it burn at a higher flow speed of about 60 to 80 cm/s (closer to buoyant flow on Earth)?

score_reasons.crew_safety: Unexplained material behaviour is a risk for screening.
score_reasons.moon_mars: Relevant to material qualification for Moon/Mars vehicles.

evidence_quote: Despite this significant heating load, the fabric was not ignited.
finding: Nomex fabric, commonly used on the ISS, did not ignite even though a burning PMMA sheet heated its base for about two minutes with an average flame power of 460 + 50 W.
material_or_fuel: Nomex fabric with a thin PMMA sheet at its base (composite sample)
conditions: Microgravity, PMMA flame heating the fabric base

values.quantity: average flame power from the PMMA

team_interpretation.text: Nomex held up against a nearby flame in this test, which supports its use, but this was one sample at one flow speed.

score_reasons.crew_safety: Supports using this common cabin fabric.
score_reasons.moon_mars: Same fabric could be used on future vehicles.

evidence_quote: On Earth, it will only burn if the oxygen concentration is increased to around 24 to 25%.
finding: Nomex HT90-40 is rated safe by NASA's standard test (NASA 6001 Test 1); on Earth it only burns if oxygen is raised to around 24 to 25%.

values.quantity: oxygen needed for Nomex to burn on Earth

team_interpretation.text: If future habitats use enriched oxygen, materials rated safe at normal oxygen need re-checking.

score_reasons.crew_safety: Shows how close cabin oxygen levels are to this fabric's burning limit.
score_reasons.evidence: Stated property used to design the test.
score_reasons.moon_mars: Exploration habitats may use enriched oxygen.

evidence_quote: Evidence that some materials which do not burn on Earth will burn in space in similar conditions
finding: NASA rates spacecraft materials with an Earth-based test (NASA-STD-6001B) and assumes a material that passes is safe in microgravity, but there is evidence some materials that do not burn on Earth burn in space.

team_interpretation.text: Passing the Earth test may not be enough on its own; space flammability data are needed for critical materials.

open_question: Which configuration, upward-spreading or downward-spreading, is more hazardous in reduced gravity? The authors say it depends on flow speed.

score_reasons.crew_safety: Questions the main material safety screen.
score_reasons.evidence: Stated as background motivation, not a result of this test.
score_reasons.moon_mars: Screening method would carry over to Moon/Mars.

evidence_quote: Fire remains a catastrophic hazard for spaceflight where the crew has very limited or no escape options.
finding: Fire is a catastrophic hazard in spaceflight because crews have very limited or no escape options, and the growth of a large fire cannot be predicted by scaling small tests linearly.

team_interpretation.text: Prevention and early control matter more than evacuation in space.

open_question: How does a large fire spread and grow inside a real spacecraft? The authors call this a substantial gap in our understanding.

score_reasons.crew_safety: The reason fire safety matters most for crews.
score_reasons.evidence: Statement of the problem, not a measurement.
score_reasons.moon_mars: Escape is even harder far from Earth.

evidence_quote: The reason for the fluctuation is unclear.
finding: The large fabric flame first pulsed in length and brightness at about 1.4 Hz, became more stable at about 90 s, then kept subtle fluctuations at around 0.75 Hz.

team_interpretation.text: A flickering flame signal is normal in microgravity; detectors should not rely on a steady signal.

open_question: Why does the flame fluctuate: a flow oscillation present even in cold flow, or the flame interacting with the flow field?

score_reasons.crew_safety: Pulsing could matter for optical fire detectors.

evidence_quote: The flame spread rate for the 5-cm-wide sample is marginally faster compared to the spread rate for the 40.6-cm-wide sample
finding: At the same 20 cm/s flow, the narrow 5-cm sample spread slightly faster than the wide 40.6-cm sample (2.1 vs 1.8 mm/s), partly because its starting oxygen was higher (22.1% vs 21.7%).

score_reasons.crew_safety: Shows small samples can overstate spread a little.
score_reasons.evidence: Measured in orbit on two sample sizes.
score_reasons.moon_mars: Sample size effects matter for test design.

evidence_quote: Average flame spread rate is 1.8 mm/s; estimated average flame power is 1200 +/- 300 W
finding: The large Saffire-1 fabric fire had an estimated average flame power of 1200 +/- 300 W and burned for 420 s in 20 cm/s air flow.

team_interpretation.text: A cabin-scale fabric fire releases about a kilowatt of heat; suppression and ventilation planning should assume fires of this size.

score_reasons.crew_safety: Heat output sizes the fire that suppression must handle.
score_reasons.moon_mars: Key input for habitat fire models.

evidence_quote: About 90% of the fuel burned in the first test leaving 10% unburned
finding: In the first large test about 90% of the 40.6 cm x 94 cm fabric burned in the 420 s allotted before the air flow was turned off.

score_reasons.crew_safety: Most of a large fabric item can burn in minutes.

evidence_quote: the air flow was shut off and the flame immediately extinguished
finding: When the air flow was shut off at the end of the about 7 min test, the large fabric flame went out immediately.

team_interpretation.text: Shutting off ventilation could be a fast first response to a fabric fire; this is our reading, not NASA guidance.

score_reasons.crew_safety: Points to ventilation control as a fast fire response.

evidence_quote: There are plans for the Saffire project to continue with additional experiments examining the effects of enhanced oxygen at reduced pressure.
finding: The Saffire project planned further experiments on fire in enhanced oxygen at reduced pressure.
open_question: How do fires spread in enhanced oxygen at reduced pressure, the atmosphere planned for exploration vehicles?

score_reasons.crew_safety: Exploration atmospheres may use this condition.
score_reasons.moon_mars: Moon/Mars vehicles may run at reduced pressure with more oxygen.
